data.title: A bronze hoard from a hillfort in the middle Váh region
data.excerpt: Society is divided over metal detectors, and so is the professional community – yet in the autumn of 2021 volunteers from the Hradiská civic association, the Trenčín Museum and the Monuments Board together rescued a hoard of 12 bronze ornaments from a hillfort newly spotted on lidar imagery. The complete set of ornaments from a woman’s costume, dated to the Late Bronze Age (12th–11th century BC) and attributed to the Lusatian culture, was lifted in a block of soil.

children.text: Just as society as a whole is divided, so the professional community too holds differing views on the use of metal detectors in the search for archaeological finds, and the level of the debate not infrequently matches this. It is, however, the deep conviction of all the authors of this article that it is the duty of all reasonable actors in the field of the protection and rescue of our shared cultural heritage to seek possible ways of cooperation between the various interested parties, whose starting positions are – let us be honest – often mutually contradictory. We are therefore going voluntarily into the lion’s den and putting our necks on the line, in the belief that we shall be presenting a pioneering way, of its kind, of rescuing an endangered past, founded on trust, competence and strict respect for the legal and ethical framework. May this article be a cultivated contribution to the never-ending debate and an illustration of what can be achieved when reasonable and rational people, united by the same goal, come together, even if the right road to the goal is always a thorny one. We trust that a certain heterogeneity of the text, which we have chosen in view of the non-academic character of the periodical in which our article is published, will not be an obstacle to the understanding of our message.

In the autumn of 2021 several members of the Hradiská civic association set out to verify a tip about a possible hillfort in the Trenčín Region. Traces of rampart defences were visible on the airborne laser scanning (‘lidar’) of Slovakia, yet a hillfort at the site in question had not been published anywhere until then, so they assumed that the site might have potential for future research. On the other hand there was also the assumption that it might be endangered by illegal searchers.

children.text: Allow us to preface the next passage of text from the authentic position of one of the members of the civic association:

After we had scrambled up a fairly high, steep hill and seen a beautifully level summit plateau with a rampart around its edge, our hearts leapt and it was immediately clear that this really was an upland hillfort. The absence of large quantities of sherds suggested that it was probably not a hillfort of the Púchov culture, which is usually ‘strewn’ with pottery. Given the proximity of Slavic sites, we rather guessed at the Slavs and other periods. In addition, below the hillfort on the opposite side, we verified the indications from the lidar that there are further ramparts there, joined to the hillfort itself, which thus forms a kind of acropolis of a fairly extensive fortification system. On the top of the hillfort there were visible pits, which could also have come from the illegal activity of detectorists.

We reported the find at once to the archaeologist of the Trenčín Museum and hoped that a rescue excavation could be arranged as soon as possible. In Slovakia the legislation governing archaeological excavations is fairly strict, and not even archaeologists themselves may go to a site and carry out excavations without the appropriate permits, above all from the regional monuments board. Under no circumstances may amateur associations such as ours carry out an excavation in such cases without a licensed archaeologist. Fortunately it did not take long before we were contacted by the archaeologist Juraj Malec, who told us that the appropriate permit had been arranged and that we could go to the excavation of ‘our’ new hillfort.

blocks.alt: A bronze hoard from a hillfort in the middle Váh region

children.text: The hoard of our dreams

So after a short time came that November morning when, full of expectation and in good spirits, we tramped up to the new hillfort with rucksacks on our backs. On arriving at the site we unpacked our gear, ground-balanced the machines and began impatiently to run around the site with our detectors. Not Peťo, though. On the way up to the hillfort he had been telling us that in the night he had dreamt a dream about finding a hoard. And about how everyone was thrilled about it, because it was a ‘Bronze Age one’. He just could not describe it to us precisely. So we had a laugh about it and wished him that it might indeed come true. Little did we know that fate would play such a beautiful trick on us and that the dream would become reality. Peťo slowly pulled his Equinox out of his rucksack and set it up. Next to him I assembled my Deus and began to wander about the hillfort. While I was still setting up, Peťo says to me: “I’ve got a signal right here.” I reply: “Sure, Peťo, go on then, give it a try.” At first it was an interesting signal, though not a clear-cut thing. One of those indeterminate things between larger iron and non-ferrous metal, which often turns out to be junk, but at the same time a signal you cannot simply leave alone and that you just have to dig. An ID of around 20 and quite a nice signal. Even though it was the first signal, and those only rarely come to anything. The rest of us gradually moved away from the starting point and so also from Peťo, who was digging away at that signal of his, and the first interesting little things were gradually starting to pop up for us. Bronze casting lumps, a small bronze bar and a pin in the shape of a bishop’s crozier, which indicated that it was probably not going to be only about the Slavs we had guessed at, but that the Final Bronze Age was taking shape here too. And Peťo still at that initial spot of his, on his knees, slowly removing the upper layers of soil, while the pinpointer was not yet reporting even a hint of a signal. But the deeper he went, the more clearly the coil on the Equinox told him that it did not look like big iron after all, but like a deep non-ferrous target. Meanwhile I had got out of Peter’s sight and picked up first a typical Slavic socketed arrowhead with two large barbs, and then a deep iron signal, which I set about digging. I went deeper and deeper until I hit massive pointed ‘projections’ on both sides, so typical of Slavic bearded axes or hoes. I was tremendously pleased that I had perhaps struck a bearded axe, and I cried out with excitement. After a few seconds, however, I heard another cry of excitement. It was coming from the direction where Peťo was digging. Immediately afterwards further cries rang out from the others who were around him. So I left my supposed bearded axe and ran to see what Peťo had there. A little knot of mates was already standing around him, debating excitedly. What have we got, lads? Could it be some green stuff? I came up to an already fairly large pit, about 45 cm deep, and it was immediately clear to me that this was a historic event for us. At the bottom of the pit two evidently twisted bronze neck rings were protruding, and in the middle of them a typical spiral ornament of the Final Bronze Age was beginning to take shape. A clear Bronze Age hoard! Heart-attack moments! The archaeologist beside himself, and we even more so. The hoard was then uncovered by Peťo together with the archaeologist. They did it very patiently and slowly. Of course a fairly large trench was made and work proceeded by layers. Gradually there appeared before us decorated bronze bracelets, further neck rings of several types, a spiral spectacle brooch, a large and beautifully decorated shield brooch and further pieces. Since it was evident that this was a large hoard of ornaments of the Final Bronze Age, the archaeologist finally decided that it would be most appropriate to lift the whole hoard in a large block and take it away with him. Its complete uncovering was then carried out in the laboratory, where even any organic remains do not escape the expert eye. The whole process of rescuing the hoard lasted practically until the evening, at the end of which we had a large and heavy block of soil with our hoard hidden inside it. The proud finder then carried it, packed up and by the light of the moon, all the way to the cars. After we got home none of us could fall asleep for a long time. And my ‘bearded axe’? In the end it turned out to be ‘only’ a beautiful Great Moravian hoe, and in its vicinity a few more arrowheads and a nice bit of silver. All these finds, however, respectfully ‘took off their hats’ to the biggest hit of the day and indeed of the year – Peťo’s hoard of women’s ornaments of the later Bronze Age, which must originally have belonged to an important Lusatian noblewoman.

children.text: A prehistoric hoard from the middle Váh region (a hoard of bronze objects from a hillfort of the Lusatian culture)

After expert cleaning it was established that the bronze hoard contained the complete set of ornaments of a woman’s costume. Of the 12 objects recovered, the dominant one was a beautifully decorated massive shield brooch, to which further ornaments were fastened, namely 2 twisted neck rings, 2 bracelets and a multi-part diadem. The hoard also contained two temple rings, a spectacle-shaped pendant, a large boss, a small boss and a further neck ring. The finds can with certainty be dated to the Late Bronze Age, that is to the 12th–11th century BC, and attributed to the bearers of the Lusatian culture.

The find of the bronze hoard and the manner of its acquisition, by means of an archaeological excavation within the framework of preventive measures to secure the protection and rescue of archaeological finds, is a unique combination of the use of an opportunity to protect our shared cultural heritage in a real way. It proved possible to discover the find thanks to the preventive activities of the Trenčín Museum in Trenčín, aimed at the rescue of archaeological finds in cooperation with volunteers from the Hradiská civic association and in coordination with the Monuments Board of the Slovak Republic. The significance of the find, moreover, does not lie only in its scholarly value as a material document of the prehistoric occupation of the Váh region. On the contrary, the whole genesis of the rescue, the exceptional cooperation, the conservation and the presentation of the find is such an example of a success story as has recently had no parallel in Slovak archaeology. We believe that, thanks to the willingness and commitment of all those involved, the story of the rescue of a prehistoric hoard from the Carpathians can serve as an outstanding example of how things can be done if we all pull together.

children.text: The rescue of the find is thus a model example of effective cooperation between actors from various spheres of cultural heritage who are, however, united by the same goal.
Significance beyond the region

The hoard from the middle Váh region is not merely a chance grouping of bronze objects, but a closed find assemblage which was lifted professionally and the whole process of which was properly documented, and it will therefore be a source of much new information. Thanks to the professional approach, the hoard has in effect been issued a ‘birth certificate’. Unlike the great majority of other bronze hoards, which come either from illegal digging or were found without the presence of an archaeologist, not infrequently as early as the 19th century, in the case of the hoard from the middle Váh region the circumstances of the find were professionally documented, which will certainly have a positive effect on the degree of certainty of its chronological classification, of its placing in the context of the occupation of the Váh region in the Bronze Age, and thus also of its final interpretation. These aspects make it a hoard of extraordinary scholarly value, whose significance, after proper professional study and publication, will extend beyond the regional boundaries of the Váh region, or of north-western Slovakia.

children.text: Cooperation of the relevant actors

The find is the result of a symbiosis and an exceptional understanding between the state, local government and the third sector. The public sphere is represented by two institutions which have the protection of cultural heritage, so to speak, in their job description. The state is represented by the Monuments Board of the Slovak Republic (or rather the Regional Monuments Board in Trenčín), with which the whole project was continuously consulted and without whose consent the rescue of the find would not have been possible. From the professional point of view, the rescue of the hoard was covered by the Trenčín Museum in Trenčín, which, thanks to its archaeologist Mgr. Juraj Malec, PhD., significantly extended its fieldwork activities beyond its traditional region as well. An archaeologist on his own, however, would not have got very far on an extensive site. Its personnel capacities were therefore, as traditionally, gladly provided by the Hradiská civic association. Thanks to the help of the members of the association in the field, who respected the instructions of the museum archaeologist, the find was not only discovered but also professionally lifted by the methods of archaeological excavation, as a preventive measure within the framework of securing the protection and rescue of archaeological finds, and thus saved for future generations. The cooperation and mutual coordination of steps thus has the character of an unconventional, but all the more desirable, solution to the current unfavourable situation with the protection of archaeological cultural heritage, which in this matter is paradoxically connected with the publication of data (lidar) to the public. The find itself, moreover, is the result of only one of several fieldwork activities whose aim is the rescue of endangered archaeological heritage in the Váh region. The Trenčín Museum in Trenčín carries out these activities, in cooperation with volunteers, over and above its basic professional duties, not infrequently outside standard working hours.

children.text: An immediate response to the possible endangering of a site as a paradigm shift towards the rescue of endangered parts of the archaeological cultural heritage

The immediate action was initiated thanks to the attentive eye of an expert who, on the newly released lidar imagery of the Váh region, spotted the existence of a hitherto unknown hillfort situated in a fairly exposed position. Several pits in the area of the hillfort suggested that the site might be an object of interest to illegal searchers. The Trenčín Museum in Trenčín therefore approached the fieldwork activities above all from the point of view of the need for an immediate response to the possible endangering of this site. At the same time, however, it was necessary to choose an approach that is in accordance with the law and with the international obligations of the Slovak Republic. Thanks to the accommodating attitude of the state authority and the willingness of the volunteers, it proved possible to find very quickly a solution that meets both the demanding requirements of professionalism and the lawfulness of the procedure, in which the rescue of the find was carried out in strict accordance with the Act on the Protection of the Monument Fund. This approach is thus at the same time a contribution by the Trenčín Museum in Trenčín to the debate on the philosophy of the approach to the protection of archaeological cultural heritage, or rather to the rescue of its endangered parts.

children.text: Rescue, conservation, presentation

The find was not only professionally lifted, but within a short time it also received the appropriate professional attention in the form of conservation. The conservation was carried out in cooperation with specialists from Masaryk University in Brno and Comenius University in Bratislava, and our thanks go to the colleagues from both institutions for their commitment and help. The conservation began while still on the premises of the Trenčín Museum in Trenčín, where the find, which had been transferred here in a block of soil, was gradually and very carefully prepared, almost under laboratory conditions. Naturally, the whole process – with a strong emphasis on an interdisciplinary approach – was (and continues to be) properly documented. After the conservation has been completed, the objects will, on the basis of cooperation with the Monuments Board of the Slovak Republic, be presented in the Trenčín Museum in Trenčín. The hoard will be published both in professional periodicals and in popularising literature. In view of the unprecedented public interest, we also anticipate a specific curatorial commentary. We regard the informal education of the public as an extraordinarily valuable aspect of our work which – as we hope – will in time be reflected in increased interest in questions of the protection of archaeological monuments and finds.

children.text: A media-friendly presentation of the public interest

The whole genesis of the rescue of the hoard can serve as a model example of the tools that can be used in the fight against illegal looting activities. Besides strict legislation, which all the actors regard as a fundamentally correct setting of the legal framework, and other repressive tools, it is also necessary to have ‘soft’ tools in the form of education, awareness-raising and media coverage. It is above all the lay public that needs to be shown that archaeological cultural heritage is really endangered every single day. In the media sphere, therefore, the public interest in the protection of archaeological cultural heritage has been repeatedly presented. With regard to the audience, which in this case is the lay public, the reference point chosen was the diametrical difference between a significant find being professionally lifted, documented, treated and presented in a publicly accessible museum collection, and such a find being stolen from a prehistoric site without even basic documentation and then disappearing into private collections, in the worse case abroad as well. The Trenčín Museum in Trenčín will continue these activities later too, in the period after the professional conservation of the find, and we shall willingly provide assistance to anyone who wishes to take part in the presentation of such good practice.
Tomáš Michalík – Juraj Malec – Peter Jenčík
